prize_parts.citation: For the development of targeted protein degradation, using small molecules that hijack the ubiquitin-proteasome system to bring a chosen protein to an E3 ligase for destruction

statement.case_for: I keep targeted protein degradation (B067) with Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli. Having read the full first round, my case rests on three things. It is a new design principle: a small molecule is built to bring a chosen protein to an E3 ligase so that the protein is removed rather than occupied, and that makes pocketless targets addressable. It is quantitative, because ternary-complex cooperativity, linker length and the VHL ligand structures can be measured and used to predict behaviour, which is what I ask of any computational or mechanistic claim. And it has been reproduced across many laboratories, ligases and targets. The chair's two questions, one achievement or two, and the third name, both have answers I can defend: the citation is written around hijacking the ubiquitin-proteasome system, and the third name is Ciulli. Five members now state B067 as their first preference and three more list it as their first alternative, so it is also the one configuration on which the committee can converge without anyone abandoning their scientific judgment.
statement.case_against: The reservations are real and I do not think they have been answered, only bounded. No degrader is approved, so the consequences are still prospective. More seriously, the three-name cut omits Handa and Ito, whose identification of cereblon as the thalidomide target is the origin of the glue strand, and also Gray, Sakamoto and Kim. A citation phrased around the ubiquitin-proteasome system covers both branches in wording but not in names, and a reader could fairly say the prize is for the PROTAC strand and describes more than it credits. If the committee concludes that the glue strand is the centre of gravity, the trio is wrong and Handa should replace Ciulli.

responses.point: Linke argues that the glue branch is not only a complication: Handa and Ito's cereblon work is the origin of the whole glue story, a citation saying only 'bifunctional molecules' may look incomplete, and he asks us to settle whether a hard cut on names is acceptable.
responses.response: You are right, and I have changed the wording as a result. My round-1 citation said 'bifunctional PROTAC molecules'; I now say that small molecules hijack the ubiquitin-proteasome system, which is accurate for both branches without crediting more than three people. On your question, I accept the hard cut on names, because three is the limit and the Nobel statutes do not allow a fourth, but I accept it knowing that Handa and Ito are left out for a serious reason and not a weak one. What keeps me from moving to Handa is that cereblon explained why an existing drug works, while the PROTAC concept and the VHL ligand and ternary-complex work gave a design rule that applies to any target. I also note that your own first-place choice, phase separation, now sits behind this one in your own ranking, which I take as a sign that principle and impact are pulling the same way here.

responses.point: Chabes keeps Crews and Deshaies but names Handa as third, arguing that the cereblon discovery unites the PROTAC and glue branches into one achievement and that degraders rely on only two or three ligases, CRBN and VHL.
responses.response: Your argument has force and I do not dismiss it. Most clinical degraders use CRBN, and without Handa's identification of cereblon that clinical progress would not have happened as quickly. But the evidence you cite for generality, that the field depends on CRBN and VHL, cuts both ways: VHL is Ciulli's contribution, and the ligand-and-structure work on it is what shows the PROTAC principle is not confined to thalidomide-like chemistry. If the prize were for glues, Handa would clearly belong; as a prize for turning ubiquitin-proteasome biology into a designable chemistry it should reach the person who made the design explicit and measurable. I have not changed my third name. I would ask you what evidence would let us choose between our two readings, because I think that is the only real disagreement left between us on B067.

responses.point: Somfai holds that C-N coupling (B013) is the clearest mature, general method with a clean two-person credit, and says that building on 2010 should not count against it because most Nobel-level methods build on earlier ones.
responses.response: That is a fair rebuke of how I put it in round 1. Building on earlier work does not disqualify a method, and your point that C-N bond formation needed its own ligand design and mechanistic work is persuasive. It is also true that no one on the committee disputes the science or the attribution of Buchwald and Hartwig, which cannot be said for any other candidate. I move B013 up to my first alternative. I still give B067 priority, because for me the 2010 prize makes the novelty margin thin in a way that is not true of a new modality, and I read the margin as a question of timing and not of quality. If the committee decides it prefers certainty of attribution to novelty, B013 is the configuration I would accept without hesitation.

responses.point: Sparr prefers phase separation (B049) and asks whether the committee wants a mature, validated advance over a concept still being tested, saying its maturity risk is of a different kind: scientific interpretation, not clinical outcome.
responses.response: That is a useful distinction, and I agree the two risks differ. Where I differ is on which risk is worse for a prize. A clinical outcome is a question of when, and the principle behind degraders is already confirmed by the structures and the biochemistry. For condensates the open question is whether many of the reported in-cell assemblies are phase separation at all, and that goes to the content of the citation. You state that candidly, and I respect it. I would not exclude a narrow B049 citation limited to liquid-like demixing as an organizing mechanism, but I do not think that is ready for a vote this year in competition with a principle whose mechanism is not in doubt. I have not changed my view, but your answer did make me more careful about describing the degrader risk as one of clinical maturity alone.

responses.point: Aili says the existence of a second glue root should not count against the PROTAC trio, because two lineages converging on one principle, chemical induction of E3-substrate proximity, can share a citation without everyone being credited by name.
responses.response: I agree with the logic and have used it in the wording. The difficulty is the one I describe above: a shared citation without shared names is honest about the science but invites the objection that Handa and Ito were excluded for convenience. I therefore want the committee to record that the cut is a judgment about which contribution is generalizable and not a finding that the glue strand is minor. On your distinction from perovskites, I agree that the credit spread over six names there is a larger allocation problem than here, so I do not press B029 in my alternatives.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts one citation covering both PROTAC and glue strands, naming only three people, or considers that a two-strand achievement cannot be fairly credited.
Whether Ciulli or Handa is the better third name; I favour Ciulli on design generality but I could be argued to Handa if the glue strand is shown to be the centre of the achievement.
Whether the lack of an approved degrader makes recognition early in 2026; I do not think it should decide the matter, but I cannot verify the current clinical status.
Whether I am giving too little weight to certainty of attribution, which favours C-N coupling over degraders.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no known tie to Crews, Deshaies, Ciulli, Handa or others on the degrader ballot, nor to the alternatives B013 and B051. My link to Arieh Warshel and the Uppsala ribosome community does not touch any shortlisted candidate. I have no recusal to declare.
